concepts.name: Service Bus duplicate detection: MessageId and the detection window
List patterns and the slice pattern
Pinning the .NET SDK with global.json and rollForward

questions.prompt: Duplicate detection is on for a Service Bus queue. After a send times out, the sender retries, and each attempt builds a new message with `MessageId = Guid.NewGuid().ToString()`. The first send had in fact succeeded. What happens?

choices.text: The second copy is dropped, since its body and queue are the same
Both copies are queued, as each attempt has its own `MessageId`
The retry fails with an exception that reports a duplicate send
Both are queued, then the receiver's peek-lock drops the copy

questions.explanation: Duplicate detection compares only the application-controlled `MessageId` within the detection window; nothing else in the message is considered. A fresh GUID per attempt makes every retry look new, so both copies are delivered. Derive the ID from the business operation (an order number plus the message subject, say) so a retry carries the same ID. A real duplicate is reported as accepted and silently dropped, not rejected.

sources.title: Azure Service Bus duplicate message detection
sources.claim: Duplicate detection tracks the application-controlled MessageId of messages sent during a time window; a new message with a logged MessageId is reported as accepted but dropped, no other part of the message is considered, and anchoring the MessageId to the business process makes it predictably repeatable.

choices.text: Nothing: it throws, as the last list pattern needs 3+ items
`one: 7`, because a list pattern checks only the first item
`7..8`, because the slice `..` can match zero elements
Nothing: it doesn't compile, as `..` can't sit in the middle

questions.explanation: A list pattern matches only when the input has exactly as many elements as its patterns, unless it has a slice. `[var x]` needs exactly one element, so `[7, 8]` fails it. The slice `..` matches zero or more elements and may sit anywhere (at most one per list pattern), so `[var first, .., var last]` matches two elements with `first = 7` and `last = 8`.

sources.title: Patterns - Pattern matching using the is and switch expressions - C# reference
sources.claim: A list pattern matches when each nested pattern matches the corresponding element; a slice pattern `..` matches zero or more elements, at most one slice may appear in a list pattern, and it can be at the start, end or middle (e.g. `new[] { 1, 0, 0, 1 } is [1, 0, .., 0, 1]` is true).

questions.prompt: During a .NET 8 to .NET 10 upgrade, builds pass on developer laptops but fail on a CI agent that has a different set of SDKs installed. How would you use `global.json` to make SDK selection predictable, and what doesn't it control?

model_answer.summary: Commit a `global.json` that pins the SDK version with a deliberate `rollForward` range, install that SDK on CI and keep the pin updated; it chooses the SDK only, not the runtime the app targets or runs on.
key_points: Without `global.json` the CLI uses the newest SDK installed on each machine, so laptops and CI agents can build with different SDKs

Commit `global.json` at the repo root with a full `sdk.version` such as `10.0.100` and a `rollForward` policy such as `latestFeature` or `latestPatch`; with a version and no policy the default is `patch`
Install the matching SDK on the CI agent and keep the pinned version current, for example with Dependabot, so you still get SDK fixes
`global.json` selects the SDK only; the APIs come from `TargetFramework` and the runtime from the runtime roll-forward rules

questions.explanation: The SDK and the runtime are chosen separately. A newer SDK can build an older target framework, so differences in installed SDKs show up as different compiler, analyzer or MSBuild behaviour between machines. Pinning a range in source control makes every machine agree, while `rollForward` keeps you from being stuck on one exact patch.

sources.title: global.json overview
sources.claim: global.json selects the .NET SDK version used by CLI commands, independently of the runtime a project targets; without it the highest installed SDK is used; sdk.version needs a full version, rollForward values include patch, latestPatch and latestFeature, and with a version and no rollForward the default policy is patch.

sources.title: Select which .NET version to use
sources.claim: SDK commands use the latest installed SDK by default unless global.json specifies one; target framework monikers define build-time APIs and framework-dependent apps roll forward at run time; consider a tool such as Dependabot to update a pinned SDK version.

questions.prompt: A Service Bus queue has duplicate detection on with the default window. An outbox relay resends an event with the same `MessageId` 30 minutes after it first sent it. What happens to the resend?

choices.text: It's queued again, as the ID is past the 10-minute default window
It's dropped, as Service Bus keeps every `MessageId` it has seen
It's dropped, as the default detection window for queues is 7 days
It's rejected, and the sender gets an error that the ID expired

questions.explanation: Service Bus remembers message IDs only for the duplicate detection window, which defaults to 10 minutes (configurable from 20 seconds to 7 days). After that the same ID counts as new, so a slow resend gets through and consumers still need to be idempotent. A larger window catches more but costs throughput, since every new ID is checked against the stored ones.

sources.title: Azure Service Bus duplicate message detection
sources.claim: The duplicate detection history window defaults to 10 minutes for queues and topics, with a minimum of 20 seconds and a maximum of 7 days; message IDs are retained only during that window, and a larger window reduces throughput.

questions.prompt: Which of these `is` expressions evaluates to `false`?
questions.explanation: Patterns before and after a slice can't share elements. `[1, 0, .., 0, 1]` needs at least four elements (two at the start and two at the end), so a three-element array fails it. The others match: a slice can match zero elements, so `[_, _, ..]` matches two items and `[.., 2, 4]` matches `{ 2, 4 }`, and `[>= 0, .., 2 or 4]` only checks the first and last items.

sources.title: Patterns - Pattern matching using the is and switch expressions - C# reference
sources.claim: The docs' examples show `new[] { 1, 1 } is [_, _, ..]`, `new[] { 2, 4 } is [.., 2, 4]` and `new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 } is [>= 0, .., 2 or 4]` as true and `new[] { 1, 0, 1 } is [1, 0, .., 0, 1]` as false.

questions.prompt: A repo's `global.json` is `{ "sdk": { "version": "10.0.100" } }`. A CI agent has SDKs 10.0.105 and 10.0.200 installed, but not 10.0.100. Which SDK does `dotnet build` use?

choices.text: 10.0.200, the newest SDK that is installed on the agent
10.0.105, the latest patch in the same feature band
None: without `rollForward`, the build needs 10.0.100
The SDK matching the runtime that the projects target

questions.explanation: With a version and no `rollForward`, the default policy is `patch`: use the specified version, or else the latest patch level in the same feature band (10.0.1xx), so 10.0.105. It won't move to the 10.0.2xx feature band without a policy such as `latestFeature`. Only `disable` demands an exact match, and the target framework doesn't choose the SDK.

sources.title: global.json overview
sources.claim: If global.json specifies an SDK version and no rollForward, patch is the default policy: use the specified version, and if it isn't found roll forward to the latest patch level, else fail; SDK versions are x.y.znn where z is the feature band; disable requires an exact match.
